prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "AMAZON COM INC" (ticker AMZN), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "AMZN", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: Amazon.com, Inc.
result.industry: E-commerce, cloud computing and digital advertising
markets: Digital advertising (retail media, Prime Video ads)
Physical grocery stores (Whole Foods, Amazon Fresh)
Consumer devices (Echo/Alexa, Kindle, Fire TV, Ring)

mission.statement: Amazon strives to be Earth's most customer-centric company, Earth's best employer, and Earth's safest place to work.
mission.plain: Amazon wants to put customers first in everything, while also being a great and safe place to work.

about.plain: Amazon runs a giant online store where you can buy almost anything and get it delivered fast, often the next day. Lots of other shops also sell their goods on Amazon's website, and Amazon stores and ships them. It also rents out huge banks of computers over the internet (Amazon Web Services) that other companies use to run their apps and AI. People pay for Prime to get free fast delivery plus movies and music.
about.customers: Hundreds of millions of shoppers, millions of sellers and advertisers, and businesses and governments that rent its cloud computers.
about.everyday: The brown Amazon boxes on doorsteps, Alexa speakers and Prime Video shows are all Amazon, and many apps you use run on AWS.

money.plain: goods it buys and sells itself online
fees for selling, storing and shipping other sellers' goods
renting computers, storage and AI tools to businesses
sponsored products and ads on Amazon, Prime Video and Twitch
Prime membership, Music, Audible, Kindle Unlimited

money.part: Amazon Leo, Zoox robotaxis and own AI chips
money.plain: satellite internet, self-driving taxis and Trainium AI chips

result.summary: Amazon has one of the widest moats in business: its unmatched fulfilment and delivery network, Prime membership flywheel and marketplace scale give it a cost and convenience edge rivals cannot easily copy, and AWS remains the largest cloud platform with high switching costs. The main risks are competition from Microsoft and Google in AI cloud, low-price Chinese marketplaces such as Temu and Shein, regulation, and the heavy AI capital spending that has pushed free cash flow negative.

pricingPower.evidence: Amazon raised the US Prime fee from $119 to $139 in 2022 without a visible loss of members, has repeatedly raised seller fulfilment and referral fees while third-party seller services kept growing about 10% a year, and advertising revenue grew 26% to $19.8B in Q2 2026; AWS pricing is more competitive, with periodic price cuts, but AWS still earned $16.6B operating income on $42.2B revenue in Q2 2026.

moats.evidence: Amazon is consistently ranked among the world's most valuable brands (top 3 in Kantar BrandZ and Interbrand rankings) and is the default starting point for US online product searches.

AWS customers build applications deep into AWS-specific services and pay data-egress costs to leave, and Prime members prepay for a year of shipping and video; sellers depend on Fulfilment by Amazon and their review history.
More shoppers attract more third-party sellers (now over 60% of units sold), which widens selection and lowers prices, which attracts more shoppers and advertisers.

Amazon operates the largest US parcel delivery network, built since 2019, and regionalised its US network in 2023 to cut cost to serve; its 2025 net sales of about $717B and capex of over $130B give it purchasing and infrastructure scale few can match.

Hyperscale cloud is effectively an oligopoly of AWS, Microsoft and Google holding about 63% of the market (Synergy, Q1 2026), because new entrants cannot fund comparable global data-centre footprints.
Amazon accepted years of thin retail margins and long-term investment that public brick-and-mortar retailers could not match without hurting their store economics.

Decades of operational know-how in robotics (over 1 million robots in its warehouses), demand forecasting and same-day logistics, plus a 'working backwards' and two-pizza-team operating culture, are difficult to replicate.

It owns custom silicon (Graviton, Trainium), a large stake in and a key compute partnership with Anthropic, exclusive content such as Thursday Night Football and the James Bond franchise, and scarce power-secured data-centre capacity.

customers.evidence: Amazon regularly tops the American Customer Satisfaction Index for online retail, Prime renewal rates have been estimated at above 90% after the first year (CIRP), and Prime Day 2025 set sales records; criticism focuses on counterfeit products and declining search quality from ads.

talent.evidence: Amazon ranked No. 1 on LinkedIn's Top Companies list for the US in several recent years and pays competitively in tech, but its demanding culture, warehouse injury criticism, return-to-office mandate and large corporate layoffs (about 14,000 in October 2025 and more in early 2026) hurt its reputation among some engineers.

product.evidence: Amazon offers the widest selection and fastest broad-based delivery in US e-commerce, AWS is ranked a Leader in Gartner's Magic Quadrant for strategic cloud platforms every year and has the broadest service catalogue, while Alexa and devices are weaker against Apple and Google.

threats: Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud, Oracle and GPU 'neoclouds' gaining AI workloads, eroding AWS's cloud share (from about 32% in 2020 to about 28% in 2026)
Capital spending of well over $150B a year on AI data centres pushed trailing free cash flow negative (-$7.6B as of Q2 2026) and may earn lower returns than expected
US FTC antitrust lawsuit (filed 2023) over marketplace practices, and EU/UK digital-markets regulation
Low-price competition from Temu, Shein and TikTok Shop, and Walmart's fast-growing e-commerce and advertising
AI shopping agents (ChatGPT, Gemini) could bypass Amazon's storefront and its advertising
Labour relations, unionisation efforts and warehouse safety scrutiny

ceo.name: Andy Jassy
ceo.background: Harvard College BA and Harvard Business School MBA; joined Amazon in 1997 and founded and ran AWS before succeeding Jeff Bezos

c1.evidence: AWS leads the fast-growing cloud and AI infrastructure market with about 28% share and revenue up 37% to $42.2B in Q2 2026.

c2.evidence: Customers choose Amazon for selection, low prices and fast free Prime delivery, backed by a logistics network and marketplace scale built over decades that rivals cannot quickly copy.

c3.evidence: Amazon is a household name worldwide, the default place many Americans start product searches, and a top-ranked company on the ACSI for online retail.

c4.evidence: Its stated mission to be 'Earth's most customer-centric company' and its Leadership Principles are emphasised constantly, but the mission is about service and efficiency rather than a grand societal purpose.

c6.evidence: “convenient, fast, everything store, huge” - the public impression is mostly positive about convenience and prices, tempered by criticism of working conditions and market power.

c7.evidence: It rides secular shifts to online shopping, cloud computing, AI and digital advertising, each multi-trillion or hundreds-of-billions-dollar markets still growing.

c8.evidence: Amazon keeps entering big markets: satellite internet (Amazon Leo), robotaxis (Zoox, launched in Las Vegas in 2025), healthcare (One Medical, Amazon Pharmacy), AI chips (Trainium) and AI models.

m1.evidence: Jassy has a clear view that generative AI and agents will reshape every customer experience and is investing heavily, but he is seen as an operator more than a visionary like Bezos.

m2.evidence: Jassy is not a founder, but as a 1997 employee who built AWS from scratch he behaves like one, keeping Bezos's 'Day 1' long-term mindset.

m4.evidence: Jassy stresses customer obsession, but large layoffs, a strict five-day office mandate and warehouse safety criticism weaken the case that he leads by serving employees.

m5.evidence: Amazon's distinctive culture of Leadership Principles, six-page memos and 'working backwards' has kept producing new products such as Bedrock, Trainium, Rufus and Alexa+ under Jassy.

m6.evidence: Jassy is deeply involved in AWS products and AI strategy, but his background is business (Harvard MBA), not engineering.

m7.evidence: Jassy is regarded as principled and low-key and continues the Climate Pledge commitments, though stewardship is focused mainly on customers and shareholders.

m7b.evidence: No commencement speech by Andy Jassy at Stanford, Harvard, MIT or a similar top university has been found.

m8b.evidence: Jassy is known as a disciplined, sports-loving manager with a lower public profile, not a larger-than-life personality like Bezos or Musk.

m9.evidence: Since 2021 he cut retail cost to serve, lifted operating income from $12.2B in 2022 to about $80B in 2025, and grew AWS into a business earning over $60B a year in operating profit.

m10.evidence: Frugality is a formal Amazon Leadership Principle, the door-desk tradition lives on, and Jassy cut management layers and bureaucracy in 2025-2026 to run 'like the world's largest startup'.

c10.evidence: Hundreds of millions of people get affordable goods delivered quickly, and millions of businesses and apps run on AWS.

p2.evidence: Running same-day delivery for hundreds of millions of items and a global cloud with custom chips is extremely hard and is core infrastructure for the modern economy.

f1.evidence: Net sales rose every year from $386B in 2020 to about $717B in 2025.

f2.evidence: Gross margin rose from about 40% in 2020 to about 50% in 2025 and operating margin from 5.9% to about 11.2%, though with a dip to 2.4% in 2022.

f3.evidence: At 30 June 2026 Amazon had $123B of cash and marketable securities against $128.9B of long-term debt and $161B of trailing operating cash flow with large positive equity, but AI capex has made free cash flow negative and debt has roughly doubled since end-2025.

f4.evidence: Operating income rose from $22.9B in 2020 to about $80B in 2025 and operating cash flow from $66B to about $140B, despite a dip in 2021-2022.

v1.evidence: For online shopping in the US, Amazon is the simplest choice: the widest selection with free, often next-day Prime delivery and easy returns.

v2.evidence: Amazon topped LinkedIn's US Top Companies list in recent years, but it is not on Fortune's 100 Best Companies to Work For and its warehouse jobs draw criticism.

c5.evidence: If Amazon vanished, shoppers would lose fast, cheap delivery, millions of small sellers would lose their main sales channel, and countless websites and apps running on AWS would go offline.
